title: Business intelligence and semantic delivery
summary: A dashboard people act on: designed backward from a decision, labelled so every number can be defended, bound to one metric contract, opened by two separate doors, honest about freshness, and proved by an acceptance script before anyone trusts it.
outcomes: Write a page's decision chain and rewrite a misleading tile label into a defensible one bound to a named metric contract.
Predict what field filters and parameters change, and write an access matrix that separates dashboard permissions, the publish-time data-permission choice and table privileges.
State freshness in words, place a refresh after the job that publishes the data, and explain what a metric view and the business-user surface add.
Compare the native AI/BI page with Power BI, Tableau and ODBC or JDBC clients, and write a storyboard and an acceptance script with independent expected values and signers.
startingAssumptions: SQL aggregation, grouping and joins are familiar; the SQL performance module's metric lesson has introduced a trustworthy metric.
The metric contract guide's unit_defect_rate definition, with its numerator, denominator, empty case and restatement rule, is the contract this module consumes rather than writes.

Unity Catalog privileges are not assumed: the permissions beat carries a short primer (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT, one GRANT example and SHOW GRANTS), and the later governance track owns the full model.
editorialRationale: Dashboard teaching fails when it starts from the tool, so the module starts from the meeting: a decision chain, then the label that makes a number defensible, then the contract every tile inherits and the controls that change it. Access is taught as two doors with the publish-time credential choice between them, freshness as a sentence and an ordering problem, and semantics as one governed definition. The business-user surface and external BI tools are placed against the same page so the learner sees what travels and what stays behind, and the storyboard and acceptance script turn the plan into evidence. Genie itself is left to its own module.

concepts.definition: The four links a dashboard exists to serve: who reads it, what they decide, what they then do, and the metric that changes that decision.
concepts.example: Line supervisors at 8 a.m. choose which line to investigate first from unit_defect_rate per line.

concepts.definition: A tile label that carries axis treatment, units, period, denominator and publish time, so a reader can say exactly what the number means.
concepts.example: 4.8% of 250 inspected units on line 3, previous business day, published 06:32.

concepts.definition: Tying a tile to a named, versioned metric contract so its dataset computes exactly the contract's grain, numerator, denominator, precision and empty rule.
concepts.example: The plant tile reads unit_defect_rate v1 as 47 over 1,040, never a mean of line rates.

concepts.definition: A dashboard control that narrows a dataset's returned rows by one of its fields, without changing what the query computed.
concepts.example: Setting line to 3 hides the other line rows; the plant dataset, which has no line field, is untouched.

concepts.definition: A named value substituted into a dataset's SQL at runtime, before aggregation, so it changes the population a query computes over.
concepts.example: Changing :business_day from 4 to 3 recomputes every line tile and the plant tile.

concepts.definition: An access level on the dashboard object itself, separate from any privilege on the tables its queries read.
concepts.example: Supervisors hold Can View on the page while SELECT on the table is a Unity Catalog grant.

concepts.definition: A publishing mode in which every viewer's queries run with the publisher's data permissions, so viewers need only access to the dashboard.
concepts.example: Published as a service principal whose data grants reach only the accepted objects, a page lets supervisors read tiles without grants of their own.

concepts.definition: A publishing mode in which each viewer's own credentials run the queries, so results depend on that viewer's access to the underlying data.
concepts.example: Cinderline's morning page shows each supervisor only what their group's SELECT allows.

concepts.definition: Words on the page naming the period covered, the publish time, whether shown days were restated, and what the page says when it was not updated.
concepts.example: Covers Tuesday. Published 06:32. Restated days are marked.

concepts.definition: A cadence or job task that re-runs a published dashboard's dataset queries and refreshes its cache, optionally sending snapshots to subscribers.
concepts.example: A 06:30 daily schedule, or a dashboard task placed after the nightly publishing task.

concepts.definition: A Unity Catalog object, defined in YAML, that holds measure definitions separately from dimensions so the aggregation is computed at query time for any grouping.
concepts.example: unit_defect_rate defined once returns 4.8% for line 3 and 4.5% for the plant.

concepts.definition: A named aggregate expression in a metric view with no fixed level of aggregation, evaluated in a query with the MEASURE function.

visuals.title: One contract, three calculations
visuals.alt: Three equations for the unit defect rate: line 3 on day 4, the plant over all lines, and the wrong average of line rates.
visuals.caption: Line 3 is 12 over 250; the plant is 47 over 1,040; the mean of four line rates is a different number the contract forbids. Synthetic teaching example.
visuals.textEquivalent:
Line 3, day 4: The contract's numerator over its denominator for one line and one business day, both summed over accepted inspections. Equation: unit_defect_rate(line 3, day 4) = 12 defective / 250 inspected = 4.8%

Plant, all lines: The same calculation over all four lines: the sums are added before dividing. Equation: unit_defect_rate(plant, day 4) = (10 + 15 + 12 + 10) / (300 + 250 + 250 + 240) = 47 / 1,040 = 4.5%

Wrong: mean of line rates: Averaging the four line rates weights a 240-unit line like a 300-unit line and prints a figure the contract does not define. Equation: (3.3% + 6.0% + 4.8% + 4.2%) / 4 = 4.6%  ≠  4.5% (not the contract)

questions.prompt: A morning-page tile reads "Defect rate 4.8" over a seven-bar chart whose axis runs from 4.0 to 5.0, with no date on the page. Which single change makes the tile defensible?

options.text: Label it with the metric contract name and version, the period covered, the unit and denominator, and the publish time, and start the axis at zero or state the truncation.
options.rationale: Each part answers an argument: what was divided by what, over which day, in which unit, and whether yesterday is in it. The value itself was never the problem.

options.text: Show 4.80 instead of 4.8 so the precision is visible.
options.rationale: Precision beyond the contract's one decimal adds nothing a reader can defend and still says nothing about period, unit or denominator.

options.text: Colour the tile red whenever it rises from the previous day.
options.rationale: A colour rule on a truncated axis and an unlabelled value amplifies the misleading reading rather than correcting it.

options.text: Replace the daily value with a seven-day rolling average to smooth the noise.
options.rationale: A rolling figure labelled as a daily rate is the most common silent labelling error; it changes the number and still leaves the label incomplete.

questions.prompt: The per-line dataset returns one row per line with unit_defect_rate. A plant tile is configured to show the AVERAGE of that column. On day 4 the rows are 3.3, 6.0, 4.8 and 4.2 per cent with inspected units 300, 250, 250 and 240 and defective units 10, 15, 12 and 10. What does the plant tile show, and is it the contract's figure?

options.text: 4.6%, and it is not the contract's figure; the contract's plant rate is 47 over 1,040, which is 4.5%.
options.rationale: The mean of the four rates is 4.575%, printed 4.6%. The contract defines the plant rate as the same calculation over all lines, sums first, which gives 4.519%, printed 4.5%.

options.text: 4.5%, the contract's figure, because averaging rates equals dividing the sums.
options.rationale: Averaging rates equals dividing the sums only when every line inspected the same number of units, which they did not.

options.text: 4.6%, and it is the contract's figure because the plant rate is defined as the mean of line rates.
options.rationale: The metric contract explicitly forbids a plant average of line rates; the plant value is the all-lines calculation.

options.text: 18.3%, the sum of the four rates.
options.rationale: A sum of rates is not a rate of anything; no widget aggregation produces a defensible plant figure from a rate column.

questions.prompt: The morning page has two datasets: per-line (line_id, business_day, rate) and plant (business_day, rate). A supervisor sets the line filter to 3. What happens to the plant tile?

options.text: It is unchanged, because a field filter reaches only datasets that return the field it is bound to, and the plant dataset has no line_id.
options.rationale: A field filter narrows results by a field the dataset returns; the plant dataset returns no line field, so the filter has nothing to act on and the plan's promise holds.

options.text: It shows line 3's rate, because a filter applies to every tile on the page.
options.rationale: A filter applies to the widgets and datasets it is connected to and only through fields those datasets return; it cannot make a plant dataset return a line.

options.text: It errors, because the filter names a field the plant dataset lacks.
options.rationale: An unconnected or unmatched dataset is simply not filtered; the documentation describes connection to widgets, not a failure mode.

options.text: It is recomputed as the plant rate with line 3 excluded.
options.rationale: Recomputation before aggregation is what a parameter substituted into the SQL does, not what a field filter on returned rows does.

questions.prompt: A supervisor has Can View on the published morning page, which was published with individual data permissions. Every tile fails for them instead of showing results. Which fix respects Cinderline's access matrix?

options.text: Restore the grants the matrix assigns the north-reporting-analysts group: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents, and SELECT on accepted.daily_line_rate and accepted.publish_status, the two objects the page reads.
options.rationale: Under individual data permissions each viewer's own grants run every dataset; SELECT is useless without USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA, and the matrix names exactly these grants for exactly this group.

options.text: Raise the supervisor's dashboard permission to Can Manage.
options.rationale: Can Manage opens more of the page door and none of the table door; the tiles would still fail under the viewer's grants.

options.text: Republish the page with the analyst's own credentials embedded so every viewer sees data.
options.rationale: That widens every viewer's reach to everything the analyst's datasets can return, including rows the matrix says supervisors must not see.

options.text: Make the supervisor a workspace admin.
options.rationale: Admin rights are neither door in the matrix and grant far more than SELECT on one table; this is the opposite of least privilege.

questions.prompt: The nightly job normally finishes at 02:10; the page's schedule runs at 06:30 and posts a snapshot to the supervisors' channel at 06:35. On Wednesday the job finishes at 08:20. What does the 06:35 snapshot show?

options.text: The older day's rows, because the schedule read the table as it stood at 06:30; only a freshness line inside the snapshot tells readers the page was not updated.
options.rationale: The schedule ran on time over the table as it was; it neither waited nor failed. Lateness becomes visible only through data the page reads about the run.

options.text: Nothing yet: the schedule waits for the job and sends at 08:20.
options.rationale: A schedule is a cadence and knows nothing about the job's completion; waiting on the job is what a dashboard task placed after the publishing task does.

options.text: An error message, because the tables were being written.
options.rationale: The queries succeed over whatever committed rows exist; a table holding the older day returns it without complaint.

options.text: The new day's rows, because a snapshot always reads the latest published data.
options.rationale: It did read the latest committed rows at 06:30, and those were the older day's; no refresh can produce rows the job has not yet published.

questions.prompt: A metric view defines unit_defect_rate as SUM(defective_units) / SUM(inspected_units) over accepted inspections, with dimensions line_id and business_day. A query selects the measure grouped by business_day only. For day 4, where the lines have defective units 10, 15, 12, 10 and inspected units 300, 250, 250, 240, what is returned?

options.text: One row for day 4 with 47 / 1,040, which is 4.5%.
options.rationale: With no line dimension the engine sums both quantities across all lines for the day and divides once: the contract's plant calculation.

options.text: One row for day 4 with 4.6%, the mean of the four line rates.
options.rationale: A metric view recomputes the ratio over sums at each grain; it never averages precomputed rates.

options.text: An error, because every dimension must appear in the grouping.
options.rationale: Dimensions are optional in a query; grouping by any subset, including none, is the point of separating measures from dimensions.

options.text: Four rows, one per line, because the line dimension is part of the definition.
options.rationale: Rows follow the query's grouping, not the definition's dimension list; grouping by day alone yields one row per day.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's analyst builds a Power BI report on accepted.daily_line_rate in Import mode using her own login and shares it to the supervisors' Power BI workspace. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Supervisors read the imported copy under Power BI's sharing; the AI/BI page's Can View list and Unity Catalog grants are not consulted when they open the report.
options.rationale: Import copies the rows into Power BI at refresh time under the analyst's credential; from then on Power BI's workspace sharing governs who sees the copy.

options.text: Unity Catalog checks each supervisor's SELECT when they open the report.
options.rationale: The catalog was consulted once, for the analyst's identity at refresh; an imported copy is read from Power BI's engine, not from the warehouse.

options.text: The report inherits the AI/BI page's connected filters and freshness line.
options.rationale: Nothing of the page travels to Power BI; slicers, a freshness caption and a schedule must be rebuilt in the report and accepted there.

options.text: Import mode is not possible; only DirectQuery works with Databricks.
options.rationale: The documentation describes both Import and DirectQuery, recommending SQL warehouses for DirectQuery; Import is supported and copies data.

selfQuestions.prompt: A plant manager asks for a page "with everything about quality". Write the four-line decision chain you would put in front of them before drawing any tile, and name one tile you would refuse and why.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Audience: line supervisors at the 8 a.m. meeting. Decision: which line to investigate first. Action: send a technician and open that line's excluded inspection. Metric: unit_defect_rate per line for the previous business day, with its exclusion counts. I would refuse the sensor-average tile: no action in the meeting depends on it and no metric contract defines it, so it would be decoration that invites argument.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The chain forces the page to serve one decision; a tile with no action and no contract fails both tests. Naming a second audience with the same numbers at the same grain, such as the plant analyst confirming at 7:30, is an acceptable addition.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline's analyst, who holds SELECT on the raw and quarantine schemas, publishes the morning page with shared data permissions. Explain what a supervisor with Can View can now reach, and what you would change before the security review.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Every dataset now runs with the analyst's grants, so a supervisor with only Can View can reach any row those datasets return, through a filter, a table view or an export, including quarantine rows if any dataset touches that schema; the catalog never checks the supervisor. Before review I would republish with individual data permissions, as the access matrix assumes, so each supervisor's own SELECT on accepted.daily_line_rate decides what they see and the quarantine link works only for stewards, and record the mode and the publishing identity in the matrix.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Shared data permissions bound exposure by the publisher's grants and the datasets, so the fix is to change whose grants run the queries, not to add a filter. Keeping shared data permissions but publishing through the API as a service principal whose data grants reach only the accepted objects the page reads is an acceptable alternative if the review records it.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write the freshness sentence for the morning page in the normal case and in the late-job case, say where it sits, and say what data it reads.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Normal: "Covers Tuesday, the previous business day. Published 06:32. Restated days are marked." Late job: "Not updated: showing Monday. See the operator note," with the note beneath. It sits at the top of the page where the eye lands, never in a tooltip. It is a tile whose dataset reads the latest successful row of the publish-run table and compares that row's business day with the expected day; the restatement mark reads the restated flag and previous value on the published table.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Both clocks, the period and the publish time, are named in words, and the not-updated state is designed rather than left to a stale timestamp. A sentence that names the job's completion time instead of a publish time is acceptable if that is what the run table records.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline's supervisors will open the morning page on a phone through the consumer surface at the 8 a.m. meeting. List what must be true of the page, the entitlements and the data grants for a supervisor to see yesterday's tiles, and what you cannot verify without a workspace.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The page must be published with individual data permissions and refreshed after the nightly job. The supervisors' group needs the consumer access entitlement, Can View on the published page and SELECT on accepted.daily_line_rate, because each supervisor's own grants run the queries; the access review also confirms whatever warehouse access the current documentation requires of viewers. Without a workspace I cannot verify the group's actual entitlement, the phone rendering of the first screen, or the exact behaviour of the consumer surface on the current release, so those are listed as unverified in the plan.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer separates the page door, the entitlement and the data door, and names what only a live workspace can confirm. Publishing instead through a least-privilege service principal with shared data permissions, so supervisors need no table grant, is an acceptable alternative design if the matrix records it.

selfQuestions.prompt: Describe, in words, the storyboard frame in which a supervisor notices that day 2 has been restated, and state what the frame must show for them to accept the number rather than argue about it.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Frame 4, 07:50, supervisors, the same page on a phone: they read the seven-day line for line 2, the line they chose first, and see a mark on day 2. The frame must show the current value 5.1%, the previous value 5.3%, the date of restatement and the reason category, all from the published table's restated flag, in the same place every time, so the supervisor reads a corrected number with its history instead of remembering a different figure from the printed report and disputing it.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The frame names the reader, the surface, the sentence read and the decision; the restatement mark with its previous value is what turns a dispute into a reading. Showing the mark in the table view only, with a hover on the chart, is acceptable if the storyboard says so.

selfQuestions.prompt: The morning page passes every acceptance row except one: line 4 on day 5 shows 0.0% where the script expects "no inspections". Explain why this is a contract failure rather than a cosmetic one, and what you change in the dataset rather than in the tile.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The contract says a line with no accepted inspections has no rate, and 0.0% asserts a perfect day that never happened; a supervisor comparing lines would rank line 4 best on a day it did not run. The failure is in the dataset: somewhere a zero denominator was coalesced to zero or a division was guarded with a default. The fix is to return NULL for the rate and let the accepted-inspection count choose the words: "no inspections" when the count is 0, as for line 4 on day 5, and "no inspected units" when inspections exist but their units total zero; the tile's formatting stays as it is, and the row is re-run after the change.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Locating the fix in the dataset keeps the tile a pure renderer of the contract and makes the correction visible to every consumer of that dataset. Adding the empty case to the metric view's definition is an acceptable alternative when the tile reads a metric view.

beats.title: A dashboard is designed backward from the action
beats.outcome: Name the audience, the decision, the action and the metric a page exists for before choosing any tile.
beats.explanation: Start from the meeting, not from the tables. Cinderline's line supervisors meet at 8 a.m. and must choose which line to investigate first; that choice is the action, and the number that supports it is yesterday's unit defect rate per line. A [[dbxfe-bi-decision-concept|decision chain]] runs audience, decision, action, metric, and a tile that sits on no link of that chain is decoration. Notice in the second state that the sensor-average tile has no action behind it and no contract under it, so it is excluded before anyone draws it.

handbook.markdown:
The first question a delivery plan asks is not which tables exist but who will act, on what, and when. Write it as four lines: the audience (line supervisors at the 8 a.m. meeting), the decision (which line to investigate first), the action (send a technician and open the excluded inspection), and the metric that changes the decision (`unit_defect_rate` per line, previous business day). Then add a fifth line the plan guide insists on: what the audience does today instead, because that is what the page must beat. At Cinderline it is two printed reports that disagree.

One page can serve two audiences only if their actions need the same numbers at the same grain. The plant analyst confirms the numbers at 7:30 and explains exclusions when asked; that is the same numbers, so the same page. The quality lead needs a count of excluded and quarantined inspections and a link to open them; that is a count and a link, not a second page.

What fails: a page with twenty tiles that answers every question and drives no decision. Sensor averages, shift counts and a plant-wide gauge each look useful and each has no action attached and no metric contract underneath, so each is removed or labelled unverified. What to inspect on an existing page: for every tile, name the action it changes; if you cannot, it is a report, and a report nobody trusts is a dispute. How to demonstrate honestly: walk the storyboard with the operations director before anything is built, and record which tile they read first.

beats.recap: Audience, decision, action, metric: a tile on no link of that chain is removed before it is drawn.

samajh.text: Socho ghar mein subah ka nashta banana hai. Pehle yeh sochte ho ki kaun khayega, kitne baje nikalna hai, aur kya banega, tab jaake fridge kholte ho. Jo pehle fridge khol kar sab kuch bahar nikaal deta hai, uska table bhar jaata hai par koi kuch khaata nahi. Dashboard bhi aisa hi hai: pehle meeting, phir decision, phir woh ek number jo decision badal de; tables uske baad.

samajh.boundary: A meal is eaten once; a page serves a repeating decision, so its metric also needs a contract and a freshness rule that breakfast never does.

beats.title: A label is part of the number
beats.outcome: Rewrite a misleading tile label into one a reader can defend, naming the five parts it must carry.
beats.explanation: A tile reading 4.8 is not a fact until its label says what was divided by what, over which period, in which unit, and when it was published. The schematic's first state is Cinderline's draft: a tile titled Defects 4.8, a bar chart whose axis starts at 4.0, a plant figure averaged from lines, and no date anywhere. The second state shows the same values under a [[dbxfe-bi-label-concept|defensible label]]: unit_defect_rate v1, previous business day, per cent of inspected units, published 06:32, restated days marked. Notice that no value changed; what changed is what a reader can defend.

handbook.markdown:
Five label parts make a rate tile defensible, and each one answers an argument that happens in the meeting.

**Axis.** A bar chart whose axis runs 4.0 to 5.0 draws a move from 4.6 to 4.8, about 4 per cent, as a bar a third taller: 0.8 against 0.6 above the 4.0 baseline. Start a rate axis at zero, or print the truncation in the axis label. **Units.** "Defects 4.8" could be a count, a rate or a percentage; write "per cent of inspected units, one decimal". **Period.** "Previous business day, plant local time" is a period; "latest" is not, and a seven-day rolling figure labelled as daily is the most common silent error. **Denominator.** The rate is defective units over inspected units of accepted inspections, so print the exclusion counts beside it: accepted, excluded, quarantined. **Freshness stamp.** The business day covered, the publish time, whether any shown day was restated, and the not-updated wording, where the eye lands rather than in a tooltip.

A useful test is to read every label aloud as a sentence: "4.8 per cent of the units line 3 inspected on the previous business day were defective; 250 inspected, 12 defective; one inspection excluded; published 06:32." If the sentence cannot be spoken, the label is missing a part. What fails without this: two percentages of different bases side by side, a plant tile that averages line rates, and a red colour rule that fires on a truncated axis. Nothing here needs a workspace; the schematic is a drawing, and a real page is checked against it by the acceptance script.

beats.recap: Axis, unit, period, denominator and freshness stamp: read the label aloud as a sentence, and if it cannot be spoken it is not a label.
beats.hint: Ask what a supervisor could wrongly conclude from each tile as drawn.

beats.title: Every tile inherits one metric contract
beats.outcome: Bind a tile to a contract by name and version and predict what the page must show for the plant figure and for an empty line.
beats.explanation: A tile is bound to a metric contract by name and version and inherits the contract's grain, numerator, denominator, precision and empty rule; it never re-derives them. The equation shows unit_defect_rate for line 3 on day 4: 12 defective units over 250 inspected is 4.8%. The plant figure is the same calculation over all lines, 47 over 1,040, which is 4.5%, never the average of line rates, which the third state shows would print 4.6%. A line with no accepted inspections shows no inspections, not 0.0%, because the contract says so, and [[dbxfe-bi-binding-concept|contract binding]] carries that rule to the page.

handbook.markdown:
Binding means the tile's dataset computes exactly what the contract defines and the tile adds nothing. Every rate tile reads one published table, `accepted.daily_line_rate`: one row per line per business day with the accepted-inspection count and the summed defective and inspected units of accepted inspections only. The per-line dataset for `unit_defect_rate` version 1 adds the rate and nothing else (shown here for one business day):

```sql
SELECT line_id,
       accepted_inspections,
       defective_units,
       inspected_units,
       try_divide(defective_units, inspected_units) AS unit_defect_rate
FROM accepted.daily_line_rate
WHERE business_day = :business_day
```

Day 4 of the five-day reconciliation sheet is Tuesday, the business day the Wednesday page covers; day 3 is Monday. The plant tile is a second dataset with the same sums over all lines: 10 + 15 + 12 + 10 = 47 defective over 300 + 250 + 250 + 240 = 1,040 inspected, which is 4.519%, printed 4.5%. Averaging the four line rates (3.3, 6.0, 4.8, 4.2) gives 4.575%, printed 4.6%, and a reader who checks the sheet will find the page wrong by a tenth and stop trusting the rest. The nightly job builds the table from the line list, because grouping inspections alone would drop a line that had none and its tile would silently vanish; that line keeps its row with a count of 0 and NULL sums, and `try_divide` returns NULL rather than raising a division-by-zero error. That NULL is what the tile renders in words, and the inspection count tells the contract's two empty cases apart: a count of 0 reads "no inspections", accepted inspections whose units total zero read "no inspected units". A COALESCE to zero at any layer breaks the contract.

What fails: a tile widget configured to aggregate a rate column, a rolling average added in the chart settings, or rounding applied twice. What to inspect: the tile's dataset SQL against the contract text, the widget's aggregation setting, and the reconciliation sheet's value for one line and one day. The restatement rule needs a column too, a restated flag with the previous value, so that the restatement mark in the freshness line has something to read. The contract itself is the metric contract guide's subject; here it is consumed, not written.

beats.recap: The tile inherits grain, numerator, denominator, precision and the empty rule; the plant figure is sums over sums, never a mean of rates.

beats.title: A filter narrows a result; a parameter rewrites the query
beats.outcome: Predict which tiles move when a viewer changes a field filter and when they change a parameter.
beats.explanation: AI/BI dashboards give a viewer two kinds of control. A [[dbxfe-bi-filter-concept|field filter]] narrows a dataset's results by a field that dataset returns; a [[dbxfe-bi-parameter-concept|dashboard parameter]] is substituted into the dataset's SQL at runtime, before aggregation, so it changes what the query computes. In the table, the line filter keeps only line 3's row from the per-line dataset, while the plant dataset returns no line field and is untouched. The third state substitutes a business-day parameter into both queries and every value moves together. Notice that a filter reaches only fields a dataset returns.

handbook.markdown:
The documentation describes filter widgets added to the canvas and connected to dataset fields, with single value, multiple values, date, date range, text entry and range slider types for field filters, and single, multiple, date and date range for parameter filters. A field filter operates on a field the dataset already returns; that is why Cinderline's plant tile, whose dataset has no `line_id` column, ignores the line filter, and why the plan guide can promise that filtering to line 3 does not change the plant figure. The filters page adds that, for relatively small datasets, field filters are often applied in the browser without re-running the query. A parameter is different: the dataset's SQL carries a named marker such as `:business_day`, the viewer's selection is substituted before the query runs, and aggregation happens after the substitution, so a parameter can change the population a sum is taken over.

Design rules that follow. Connect each filter deliberately to the widgets it should govern; an unconnected tile is not a bug but a decision to record. Prefer a parameter when the value must reach the WHERE clause before aggregation (the business day), and a field filter when the viewer is choosing among rows the dataset already computed (the line). Refuse free-text filters on the morning page: there is nothing to type that the two allowed selections do not cover, and a free-text filter invites a search for rows the viewer should not see. Query-based parameters, which draw their allowed values from a dataset, are the documented way to offer a list that follows the data.

What to inspect when a tile does not respond: the filter's connections, the field name the filter is bound to, and whether the dataset returns that field at all. A filter is a reading aid and not a security boundary; the permissions beats say why.

beats.recap: Field filters narrow returned rows by a field the dataset has; parameters are substituted into the SQL before aggregation.

beats.title: The page and the data have separate doors
beats.outcome: Write an access matrix that separates a principal's dashboard permission from its privileges on the underlying tables.
beats.explanation: A dashboard has its own permission levels, Can View to Can Manage, and the tables behind it carry Unity Catalog privileges. Those are two doors, and a [[dbxfe-bi-permission-concept|dashboard permission]] opens only the first. The matrix shows Cinderline's principals: the analysts group views the page and can read the two accepted objects it queries, the stewards also reach the quarantine table, the data team edits, the nightly job's principal writes the table with no page door, and everyone else has neither. Notice in the second state that revoking the analysts' SELECT leaves the page door open yet breaks their tiles, because the page runs each viewer's own grants.
beats.recap: Can View, Can Run, Can Edit, Can Manage open the page; only Unity Catalog privileges open the tables, and neither door grants the other.
beats.hint: A permission on an object never implies a privilege on what the object reads.

beats.title: Embedded credentials make the publisher the reader
beats.outcome: Choose between embedded and individual data permissions for a page and name what each choice exposes and requires.
beats.explanation: When a dashboard is published, the publisher chooses whose data permissions run its queries. With [[dbxfe-bi-credentials-concept|embedded credentials]], the documented shared data permissions option, every viewer's query runs as the publisher, so the catalog checks the publisher's grants and a viewer needs only Can View. With [[dbxfe-bi-viewer-credentials-concept|individual data permissions]], each viewer's own grants are checked and a viewer without SELECT gets no results. Follow the request in the diagram: the privilege check moves from the publisher to the viewer. Notice that under embedded credentials a filter is not a wall; whatever the publisher's queries can return, a viewer can reach.

handbook.markdown:
The share documentation describes the publish step as a choice, with shared data permissions the default: share data permissions, where the publisher's credentials determine access to the underlying data and queries run with the publisher's permissions, or individual data permissions, where each viewer must have explicit access to the underlying data to see results. The API exposes the same choice as `embed_credentials` on the publish call, and the API tutorial shows publishing as a service principal: obtain an OAuth token for the principal, call publish with `embed_credentials` true, and viewers then use the principal's permissions for data and compute while needing permission only on the dashboard object; the tutorial adds that audit logs then show the principal as the query executor.

The trade is exposure against administration. Embedded credentials mean one identity's grants to maintain, a shared result cache that a schedule refreshes, and no per-viewer table privileges; they also mean that every row the publisher's datasets can return is reachable by anyone with Can View, through a filter, a table view or an export. If the publisher is a human analyst with SELECT on raw and quarantine schemas, the page has quietly widened that person's access to every viewer. Individual permissions mean each viewer needs the table grants and whatever compute access the current page requires, more administration and a per-user cache rather than a shared one, but the catalog decides per person.

Cinderline's rule: publish the morning page with individual data permissions, because the access matrix already grants each group exactly the rows it may read and the page must not widen that; the price is a per-user cache and grants to maintain. The quarantine link then works only for stewards who hold SELECT on the quarantine table. Shared data permissions would be defensible only through the API as a service principal whose data grants reach only the accepted objects the page reads, and never from a personal login: the data team's development grants reach raw and quarantine schemas, and they leave when a person does. What to inspect: the published page's data-permission mode, the identity it was published as, and that identity's grants.

beats.recap: Embedded credentials check the publisher's grants for every viewer; individual permissions check each viewer's own; embed only a least-privilege service principal, never a personal login.
beats.changeNote: Corrected: this beat had called SELECT on the accepted table a publishing service principal's only grant. The Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 API reference (commit 9df82c7) shows it needs more: publishing requires the Databricks SQL access entitlement, and querying a table also needs USE_CATALOG and USE_SCHEMA. The beat now says the principal's data grants reach only the accepted objects the page reads, one identity's grants to maintain.

samajh.text: Socho ek society ka guard aur ek flat ki chaabi. Guard gate pe naam check karke andar aane deta hai; yeh page ka Can View hai. Par flat ke andar kya dikhega, woh chaabi tay karti hai. Embedded credentials ka matlab: page banane wale ne apni chaabi darwaze pe hi latka di, ab jo bhi gate paar kare, usi chaabi se saare kamre khol sakta hai. Individual permissions mein har mehmaan apni chaabi laata hai, aur jiske paas nahi hai, woh darwaze pe hi ruk jaata hai.
samajh.mapping: The guard is the dashboard's Can View permission, the flat is the set of underlying tables, and the key hanging on the door is the publisher's credential embedded at publish time.
samajh.boundary: A key opens every room of the flat, whereas embedded credentials expose only what the page's datasets return, so the exposure is bounded by the datasets and the publishing identity's grants, not by every table the publisher can read.

beats.title: Freshness is a sentence the reader can act on
beats.outcome: Write the freshness statement for a page in its normal and not-updated states and say what data it reads.
beats.explanation: A timestamp in a corner tells a supervisor nothing about whether yesterday is in the numbers. A [[dbxfe-bi-freshness-concept|freshness statement]] says, in words where the eye lands, which business day the page covers, when it was published, that restated days are marked, and what the page says when it was not updated. The timeline runs from the plant's day through the 02:10 nightly job and the 06:30 refresh to the supervisors' 07:45 read before the 8 a.m. meeting. In the second state the job finishes after the meeting, and the page must say not updated, showing Monday, not Monday's rows under Tuesday's heading.

handbook.markdown:
Freshness has two clocks that readers confuse: the period the numbers cover and the moment they were published. The plan guide puts both in words at the top of the page: "Covers Tuesday (the previous business day). Published 06:32. Restated days are marked." When the nightly run has not published by 7:30, the same position reads "Not updated: showing Monday. See the operator note," and the note appears beneath it. A report held while a conflicting inspection is adjudicated uses the same position with its own reason, "Held: conflict under adjudication", and the owner's note. A refresh timestamp alone would have said 06:30 on both mornings and been true both times, which is the problem.

The statement is a tile like any other, and it needs a dataset. The nightly job writes one row per run to `ops.publish_run` with the business day it published, the completion time and a status. The page reads it through `accepted.publish_status`, a view over that table published beside the rate table, so a reader's grants stay inside the accepted schema. The freshness dataset reads the latest successful row and compares its business day with the expected one:

```sql
SELECT business_day, completed_at,
       CASE WHEN business_day = :expected_day THEN 'current'
            ELSE 'not updated' END AS state
FROM accepted.publish_status
WHERE status = 'published'
ORDER BY completed_at DESC LIMIT 1
```

The restatement mark reads the `restated` flag and previous value that the contract requires the published table to carry, so a day changed since it was first shown is marked with what it replaced. What fails: a page whose header is typed text rather than a dataset, which says Tuesday forever; a freshness line in a tooltip; and a late job that nobody is told about, which the plan's ownership row fixes by notifying the operator and the analyst before 7:30. What to inspect on a doubtful morning: the latest `publish_run` row, the published table's maximum business day, and the schedule's last run time, in that order.

beats.recap: Period covered, publish time, restatement mark and the not-updated wording, read from a run table, where the eye lands.

samajh.text: Akhbaar par sirf 'chhapa 5 baje' likha ho toh kya fayda? Padhne wale ko chahiye: yeh kal ki khabar hai ya parso ki, aur agar aaj ka akhbaar hi nahi aaya toh kya kal wala rakha hai. Dashboard ki freshness bhi ek line mein bolo: kaunsa din, kab chhapa, kya badla, aur agar nahi aaya toh saaf likha ho ki purana dikh raha hai.
samajh.mapping: The newspaper's date line is the period covered, the print time is the publish time, a corrections box is the restatement mark, and today's edition not delivered is the not-updated state.
samajh.boundary: A printed edition is never changed in place, while a dashboard's day can change on the next run, so the mark and the previous value matter more than they do in print.

beats.title: A refresh cannot make data newer than its source
beats.outcome: Place a dashboard refresh relative to the job that publishes its table and predict what a snapshot and the page show when the order is wrong.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-bi-refresh-concept|refresh schedule]] re-runs a page's dataset queries on a cadence, refreshes the shared cache when the page uses shared data permissions, and can send subscribers a snapshot by email, Slack or Microsoft Teams. What it cannot do is produce rows the nightly job has not published. In the diagram, a 06:30 refresh after a 02:10 job snapshots Tuesday; the same refresh before a job that finishes at 08:20 snapshots Monday and posts it to the supervisors' channel at 06:35 without a word. Notice that the trigger belongs after the job, not on the clock.

handbook.markdown:
The schedule documentation describes a periodic cadence: at each scheduled update all the SQL that defines the datasets runs, and for a page published with shared data permissions the shared cache is refreshed. Subscribers additionally receive a snapshot by email, Slack or Microsoft Teams, and a subscriber can choose to refresh data without receiving the email. Each run executes the page's dataset queries on the dashboard's warehouse, or on the warehouse the schedule itself names, so it costs compute and returns whatever the tables hold at that moment.

That last clause is the design constraint. Cinderline's nightly job normally completes at 02:10; the page's schedule runs at 06:30 and posts a snapshot to the supervisors' Teams channel at 06:35. On a slow night the job finishes at 08:20. The schedule does not wait, does not fail and does not know the job was late: it snapshots Monday's rows and posts them on Wednesday morning with no operator note. Supervisors who open the page at 07:45 run their own queries under individual data permissions and see what the table holds, which is still Monday.

Two mitigations belong together. First, make the freshness line read the publish-run table, so lateness is visible in words on the page and inside every snapshot. Second, trigger the refresh from the job rather than the clock: the documented dashboard task, added to the nightly job after the publishing task, refreshes the dashboard and can send a snapshot to its own subscriber list, and it needs a serverless or pro SQL warehouse. Where that is not available, the schedule sits after the job's expected completion plus a buffer that the operator reviews when the job's duration drifts.

What to inspect on a doubtful morning: the schedule's or task's last run time and warehouse, the published table's maximum business day, and the snapshot's send time relative to the job. A per-user cache under individual data permissions is a cost and permission question, not a freshness one.

beats.recap: A schedule or snapshot shows whatever the table holds when it runs; trigger it after the job and let the freshness line say when it ran early.
beats.changeNote: Corrected this beat's handbook, which had said every scheduled run uses the dashboard's warehouse: it now says a run uses the dashboard's warehouse or a warehouse the schedule itself names. Source: Databricks SDK for Python 0.141.0 API reference (commit 9df82c7), where a dashboard schedule has its own optional warehouse_id field.

beats.title: A metric view defines the measure once for every grain
beats.outcome: Explain what a metric view separates and predict its result for a line-level and a plant-level query.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-bi-metricview-concept|metric view]] is a Unity Catalog object that separates [[dbxfe-bi-measure-concept|measures]], the numbers defined once as expressions such as the sum of defective units over the sum of inspected units, from dimensions, the fields you group and filter by. A query names a measure and any dimensions, and the engine computes the ratio over the sums for that grouping. The table shows one definition answering a line question and a plant question: 4.8% for line 3 and 4.5% for the plant, never the 4.6% mean of rates. Notice that the contract's numerator and denominator now live in one governed definition that dashboards and other clients share.

handbook.markdown:
The documentation describes metric views as the core of Unity Catalog semantics: measure definitions are separated from the dimensions used to group, filter and aggregate them, the definition is written in YAML and registered in Unity Catalog through SQL or Catalog Explorer, and a query can group by any available dimension while the engine generates the correct computation. A standard view locks its aggregation at creation time; a metric view defers it to the query. Schematically, the definition names a source, dimensions with expressions, and measures with aggregate expressions:

```yaml
# schematic shape; the YAML reference owns the exact keys, including the version key it requires first
source: quality_pilot.accepted.daily_line_rate
dimensions:
  - name: line_id
    expr: line_id
  - name: business_day
    expr: business_day
measures:
  - name: unit_defect_rate
    expr: try_divide(SUM(defective_units), SUM(inspected_units))
```

A query then asks for the measure at a grain: grouped by `line_id` it returns 4.8% for line 3; with no dimension it returns 47 over 1,040, which is 4.5%, because the ratio is recomputed over sums at each grouping. That is exactly the contract's plant rule, now enforced by the object rather than by every dashboard author remembering it. The documentation names a `MEASURE` function for selecting a measure in a query; check the current syntax page before writing one.

An AI/BI dataset can be based on a metric view directly, so the page's tiles read the governed definition instead of copying its SQL. What a metric view does not do: it does not decide the empty rule by itself (`try_divide` keeps a zero denominator as NULL, and the tile still has to show it in the contract's words, "no inspections" or "no inspected units"), it does not carry the restatement mark, and it helps only a client that sends SQL to the warehouse; a BI tool with its own semantic model re-expresses the definition and must be reconciled by the acceptance script. What to inspect: `DESCRIBE` the view, compare each measure's expression to the contract text, and run the two-grain query above against the reconciliation sheet.

beats.recap: Measures defined once, dimensions chosen at query time, the ratio recomputed over sums at every grain; the contract lives in the catalog.

samajh.text: Halwai ke paas ek recipe card hota hai: 'ek kilo besan pe itna ghee, itni cheeni'. Chahe do kilo banao ya bees, anupaat wahi rehta hai, kyunki card anupaat likhta hai, taiyaar plate nahi. Metric view bhi recipe card hai: rate ka formula ek baar likha, aur line, plant ya poora mahina, jis bhi size pe poochho, formula wahi lagta hai aur jawab us size ke liye naya nikalta hai.
samajh.mapping: The recipe card is the metric view's measure definition, the batch size is the grouping dimension, and the ratio of ingredients is the ratio of sums the engine recomputes for each grouping.
samajh.boundary: A recipe scales linearly by design, while a metric view recomputes a ratio over sums, so a larger grouping is not a scaled copy of a smaller one and can differ from the mean of its parts.

beats.title: AI/BI meets the business user where they read
beats.outcome: Describe the business user's path to a published page and what must be true of the page, the entitlement and the grants for it to work.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-bi-aibi-concept|AI/BI]] is the documentation's name for dashboards, Genie and the consumer experience built on the same governed tables. A supervisor does not open a workspace: the documentation describes [[dbxfe-bi-genie-one-concept|Genie One]], formerly Databricks One, as the simplified interface where business users view AI/BI dashboards, ask questions in natural language and run Databricks Apps, with consumer access as the least-privileged option. The comparison sets the supervisor's path beside the author's. Notice that the page, its permissions and its freshness line are one object on both paths; only the surface differs. Genie's natural-language answers belong to the Genie module and are only a neighbour here.

handbook.markdown:
The AI/BI overview lists three things: dashboards, described as low-code with visualizations and cross-filtering; Genie Agents, domain-specific environments where data teams configure trusted data, metrics and business rules that power Genie One answers; and Genie One, the simplified UI for business users to view AI/BI dashboards, ask questions in natural language and run Databricks Apps. The Genie One page adds that it was previously known as Databricks One and that consumer access, the least-privileged option, is enough for its chat. Names in this family have changed more than once, so the release-notes page is the place to check what the current names are before writing a runbook.

For Cinderline's supervisors the path is: an entitlement that admits them to the consumer surface, Can View on the published page, and, because the page is published with individual data permissions, SELECT on the accepted table through their group. The author's path is the workspace: the draft, the datasets, the publish dialog and the schedule, worked with the data team's own grants. On the quarantine link, the steward's own SELECT on the quarantine table decides.

What the business user can do on the page: read the tiles, use the connected filters, subscribe to the schedule, and, where a Genie Agent is configured for the same data, ask a question in words. What they cannot: edit a tile, change a definition, or see a row their own grants do not allow. What to verify with a workspace, and only there: the analysts group's entitlement, the phone rendering of the first screen, and the exact consumer-surface behaviour on the current release. How to demonstrate honestly without one: walk the storyboard over the schematic page and say which steps are unverified.

beats.recap: Dashboards, Genie and the consumer surface share one governed page; a business user needs an entitlement, Can View and, on Cinderline's page, their group's SELECT, not a workspace.

beats.title: A storyboard rehearses the meeting before the page exists
beats.outcome: Draw a morning meeting as frames that each name a reader, a surface, a sentence read and an action taken.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-bi-storyboard-concept|storyboard]] is the meeting drawn as frames: who opens what, reads which sentence, chooses what, and where they go next. Cinderline's morning runs in five frames: the analyst confirms the numbers at 7:30, the supervisors open the page at 7:45, read the freshness line, compare four line tiles and choose line 2, the highest at 6.0%, and the quality lead opens the excluded inspection. The second state is the same meeting on a not-updated morning. Notice that every frame names the tile it reads and the action it produces, which is how a storyboard exposes a tile nobody reads.

handbook.markdown:
A storyboard frame has six fields: time, actor, surface, what is read, what is decided, and where the actor goes next. Cinderline's morning page, drawn before it is built:

| Frame | Time | Actor | Surface | Reads | Decides / next |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 07:30 | Plant analyst | Workspace | Freshness line, line 3 tile, counts | Confirms against the sheet; notes exclusions |
| 2 | 07:45 | Supervisors | Phone, consumer surface | Freshness line first | Trusts the day, or reads the operator note |
| 3 | 07:47 | Supervisors | Same page | Four line tiles, seven-day lines | Line 2 first: 6.0%, 15 of 250 |
| 4 | 07:50 | Supervisors | Same page | Line 2's seven-day line, day 2 marked | Accepts 5.1%, previous 5.3%, no argument |
| 5 | 08:05 | Quality lead | Quarantine page | Excluded count and link | Opens the excluded inspection |

The not-updated variant replaces frame 2's sentence with "Not updated: showing Monday" and frame 3 with a decision to use Monday knowingly or wait for the operator. Drawing it shows what the page must do on that morning, which is the case most pages never design for.

Each frame becomes a row of the acceptance script: frame 3 is the four tile values, among them "line 3, day 4 equals 4.8%", and line 2 ranking first; frame 4 is "line 2's day-2 mark shows 5.3%"; frame 5 is "the quarantine link is refused under the analyst identity". Frame 2 on a phone decides the layout: the freshness line and the four tiles must fit the first screen at 390 pixels, so the seven-day lines go below. What fails: a storyboard that is a list of screenshots, which names no sentence and no decision; and a storyboard reviewed only by the builder. Review it with the operations director and the plant analyst, ask them to point at the tile they would read first, and write down what they did today instead.

beats.recap: Time, actor, surface, sentence read, decision, next: five frames plus the not-updated variant, each becoming an acceptance row.

beats.title: External BI tools read the warehouse, not the page
beats.outcome: State what Power BI, Tableau and an ODBC or JDBC client each do with a Databricks table and which parts of an AI/BI page do not travel with them.
beats.explanation: Power BI, Tableau and any ODBC or JDBC client connect to a SQL warehouse under their own identity and read tables and views through Unity Catalog. That is [[dbxfe-bi-external-concept|external BI integration]]: the documented connectors, Partner Connect and the [[dbxfe-bi-driver-concept|ODBC and JDBC drivers]] carry queries, not pages. The comparison table shows what travels, SQL, catalog privileges and a metric view as an object, and what does not, the AI/BI page's permissions, its filters, its freshness line and its schedule. Notice that a Power BI report of the same table is a second page that needs its own labels and its own acceptance script.

handbook.markdown:
**Power BI.** The documentation covers connecting Power BI Desktop through Partner Connect, manually with the server hostname and HTTP path, or through the Power BI Delta Sharing connector; publishing data from Databricks to the Power BI service; and orchestrating semantic-model refreshes with a Power BI task. The Desktop page recommends SQL warehouses for DirectQuery, where each visual sends live SQL, and describes Import, where the data is copied into Power BI's engine at refresh time. The page lists the current authentication methods, which include OAuth for a user and a service principal's credentials for unattended refresh, and the connector supports the ADBC driver as an alternative to ODBC. In Import mode the copy leaves Unity Catalog's reach: Power BI's own workspace sharing and row-level rules govern who sees it, and freshness is the semantic model's last refresh.

**Tableau.** Partner Connect connects a SQL warehouse to Tableau Desktop in a few clicks; Tableau Cloud can create data sources from Unity Catalog tables from the Databricks side; a manual connection takes the hostname, HTTP path and an authentication method. Live connections send SQL per interaction; extracts copy, with the same consequences as Import.

**ODBC and JDBC.** Databricks provides an ODBC driver and a JDBC driver for any other tool; the connection string names the host, HTTP path and authentication mechanism. The drivers page notes that some tools need the ODBC driver installed, Tableau Desktop among them, while recent Power BI Desktop releases include it. Every client above runs as the identity in its connection, so the catalog's grants apply to that identity and nothing else does.

What does not travel: the AI/BI page's Can View list, its data-permission choice, its connected filters and defaults, its freshness dataset and its schedule. A metric view is a catalog object, so a client that passes SQL through can query it; a tool with its own semantic layer re-expresses the measure and must be reconciled. Cinderline's supplier contact who wants line 2 in Tableau therefore gets a grant on a view that returns only line 2, a separate acceptance row, and a freshness caption written in Tableau, not a copy of the page.

beats.recap: Connectors and drivers carry SQL under their own identity; the page's permissions, filters, freshness line and schedule stay behind.

beats.title: An acceptance script names the value before the page shows it
beats.outcome: Write an acceptance script with expected values from outside the page, the states to try and who signs each row.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-bi-acceptance-concept|acceptance script]] is written before the page exists: a fixed input snapshot, the exact value every tile must show, the filter states to try, the empty, restated and not-updated cases, the identity tests, and who signs which row. The table's first state lists Cinderline's script with expected values from the five-day reconciliation sheet; the second is the same script after a run, with one failure: line 4 on day 5 shows 0.0% where the contract says no inspections. Notice that a script whose expected values were copied from the page could never fail.

handbook.markdown:
The script has one row per check, and each row has an expected value that exists before the page does. Cinderline's rows come from the plan guide, on the retained five-day synthetic snapshot: line 3 on day 4 equals 4.8% to one decimal; the counts beside line 2's day-2 tile equal 20 accepted, 1 excluded, 1 quarantined; after the day-4 correction line 2's day-2 restatement mark appears with the previous value 5.3%; a line with no inspections on day 5 shows "no inspections", not 0.0%; filtering to line 3 leaves the plant tile at 4.5%; the page under a test analyst identity shows the tiles and refuses the quarantine link; the page under the outsider identity does not load. Three signers: the plant analyst for values, the quality lead for counts and marks, the security lead for access.

Running it means loading the snapshot into a test schema the page's datasets can be pointed at, opening the page under each identity, and recording observed values with the date and the identity used. The not-updated case is simulated by pointing the freshness dataset at a `publish_run` row for the wrong day. Every failure is recorded against the row, and the fix is made in the dataset, not in the tile: the 0.0% failure above means a COALESCE crept into the empty case, and the cure is the NULL the contract requires. Re-run the whole script after each metric contract version, not only the row that changed.

What fails: acceptance by looking, expected values copied from the page, a script run only by its author, or a script with no identity rows. How to explain it: the script is the plan's promise turned into evidence, and the signatures say who checked which promise. How to demonstrate honestly: attach the run log with observed values; a page with no run log is not accepted, however right it looks.

beats.recap: Expected values from the reconciliation sheet, states and identities to try, signers per row, and a run log; fix failures in the dataset.
beats.hint: Ask where each expected value came from; if the answer is the page, the row proves nothing.

extensionCards.prompt: Why do supervisors on a page with shared data permissions all see the same numbers, and when might one of them not?
extensionCards.answer: They read one shared cache the schedule refreshed; a draft, or a page under individual data permissions, keeps a per-user cache instead.
extensionCards.explanation: Dashboards keep a best-effort [[dbxfe-bi-extension-caching-concept|result cache]] for 24 hours. A page published with shared data permissions uses one cache for every viewer, which a scheduled update populates, so every viewer reads the 06:30 result. Under individual data permissions, which Cinderline's morning page uses, each viewer's queries fill their own cache, so two supervisors opening the page minutes apart can see results from different moments. Because the cache is best effort, the freshness line must read the run table rather than assume the cache is current.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Explains why one publishing choice also decides whether the whole meeting sees one result or several.

extensionCards.prompt: What happens to Can Edit granted to someone who is in the Databricks account but not in the workspace?
extensionCards.answer: The sharing dialog shows it, but their actual permission on the page is limited to Can Run.
extensionCards.explanation: A published dashboard can be shared with [[dbxfe-bi-extension-account-share-concept|anyone registered to the Databricks account]], even without workspace access, which is how a plant contact outside the data team can read it. The documentation states that such users are limited to Can Run whatever higher level appears in the dialog, so an access review lists the effective level, not the displayed one. The data door is unchanged: under shared data permissions the publisher's grants still decide what they can reach.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Prevents an access review from recording a permission a user cannot actually exercise, or missing a reader outside the workspace.

extensionCards.prompt: How can the line 2 page reach a supplier's own portal without giving the supplier's staff Databricks accounts?
extensionCards.answer: Through embedding for external users: a service principal with read access authorizes the page, and the portal's server issues each viewer a short-lived scoped token.
extensionCards.explanation: [[dbxfe-bi-extension-embedding-concept|Embedding for external users]] places a published dashboard in an external application for viewers without Databricks accounts. The service principal is granted read access to the dashboard and its underlying data, the application's server exchanges the principal's secret for a token and then a token scoped to the individual viewer, and those tokens last one hour. The exposure question is the one this module asks of embedded credentials: the principal's grants bound what any viewer can see, so it gets a view of line 2 only. Availability is checked on the current page before design.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Shows that external delivery is an identity design, not a link, and reuses the least-privilege publishing rule.

extensionCards.prompt: How can an acceptance script record a filtered state so a second tester opens exactly the same view?
extensionCards.answer: By recording the published page's URL, which stores the field filter and parameter selections, and opening that link.
extensionCards.explanation: A published dashboard writes its field filter and parameter selections into the [[dbxfe-bi-extension-filter-url-concept|page address]], so a bookmarked or shared link reopens with those values applied. An acceptance row such as "line = 3, business day 4, plant tile 4.5%" can therefore carry the exact link the tester used, and a supervisor's bookmark opens the meeting's state. The link records selections, not permissions: a viewer without access still cannot open it.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Makes filter states reproducible evidence rather than a description of clicks, and warns that a link is not an access grant.

recap.title: Audience, contract, two doors, one clock, a script
recap.markdown: **A page is worth building only when an audience makes a decision from it.** Write the decision chain first, then label every tile so it can be read aloud as a sentence: unit, period, denominator, axis and freshness. Bind each tile to one metric contract, so the plant figure is a ratio of sums and an empty line says no inspections. Filters narrow returned rows; parameters rewrite the query. The page door (Can View to Can Manage) and the data door (table privileges) are separate, and the publish-time choice decides whose grants run the queries: Cinderline runs each viewer's own, and a shared publisher is only ever a least-privilege service principal. A refresh cannot make data newer than the job that published it, so put it after the job and say freshness in words. A metric view holds the contract in the catalog; Genie One is where business users read the page; Power BI, Tableau and ODBC or JDBC clients read the warehouse, not the page. An acceptance script with outside values and signers is the proof. **Transfer challenge:** redraw the schematic dashboard for a hospital's morning bed-occupancy huddle, naming the contract's denominator, the not-updated wording and the one access-matrix row that would leak patient-level rows if the page were published from the wrong identity.

appliedTask.title: The South plant joins the morning page
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline's South plant adopts the morning page. Its nightly job usually finishes around 04:40 plant local time, its supervisors meet at 7:00, its three lines report to the same unit_defect_rate contract, and its quality stewards must not see North's quarantine rows. The finance controller also wants South's rate in an existing Power BI report refreshed in Import mode. Write the decision chain, the freshness statement in both states, the access-matrix rows that change, how the plant and two-plant figures are computed, the refresh order, four acceptance rows with their source and signer, and what the Power BI report needs that the page does not give it.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Decision chain: South supervisors at 7:00 choose which of their three lines to investigate first; action, send a technician and open that line's excluded inspections; metric, unit_defect_rate v1 per line, previous business day. Freshness: "Covers Tuesday. Published 06:05. Restated days are marked."; late: "Not updated: showing Monday. See the operator note." Access: a south-reporting group with Can View and SELECT on South's accepted rows only; south-stewards with SELECT on South's quarantine only; the page stays under individual data permissions, so each group's own grants decide and North's groups gain nothing. Figures: South is the sum of South's defective units over the sum of its inspected units; any two-plant figure is sums over sums, never a mean of plant rates; both come from the metric view. Refresh: a dashboard task after South's publishing task, since a single 06:30 schedule would miss the 7:00 meeting on a late night. Acceptance rows from South's reconciliation sheet: one line value, the South plant value, an empty line reading no inspections, and the North steward identity refused South's quarantine link, signed by the South analyst, quality lead and security lead. Power BI: its own connection identity with SELECT on the accepted view only, its own freshness caption from the semantic model's refresh time, a refresh scheduled after the job, the measure re-expressed or read from the metric view by SQL, and its own acceptance row, because none of the page's permissions, filters or freshness travel.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer changes only what South changes, the time, the audience, the grants and the order, and keeps the contract, the empty rule and the ratio-of-sums rule fixed. It treats Power BI as a second page with its own identity, freshness and acceptance rather than as a copy of the first.
